title: The puppets recognise their brother Pinocchio and give him a wonderful welcome; but just at the best moment the puppet master Fire-Eater appears, and Pinocchio is in danger of a terrible end.
paragraphs: When Pinocchio entered the little puppet theatre, something happened that caused almost a revolution.
You must know that the curtain was up and the play had already begun.
On the stage, Harlequin and Punchinello were quarrelling and, as usual, threatening at any moment to exchange a load of slaps and blows with sticks.

The audience, watching closely, was laughing itself sick at the argument between the two puppets, who waved their arms and called each other every rude name so convincingly that they might have been two thinking creatures, two real people in this world.
When all at once, out of the blue, Harlequin stops acting, turns towards the audience, points to someone at the back, and begins shouting dramatically:
“Gods of the heavens! Am I dreaming or awake? Why, that’s Pinocchio over there!…”
“It really is Pinocchio!” cries Punchinello.
“It’s him!” shrieks Miss Rosaura, peeping out at the back of the stage.
“It’s Pinocchio! It’s Pinocchio!” all the puppets shouted together, leaping out from the wings.
“It’s Pinocchio! It’s our brother Pinocchio! Hooray for Pinocchio!…”
“Pinocchio, come up here to me!” cries Harlequin. “Come into the arms of your wooden brothers!”

At this loving invitation, Pinocchio gives a leap from the back of the theatre to the best seats; then with another leap he jumps from the best seats onto the head of the orchestra conductor, and from there springs onto the stage.

It is impossible to imagine the hugs, neck squeezes, friendly pinches, and head bumps of true, heartfelt brotherhood that Pinocchio received in the great tangle of actors and actresses from that wooden theatre company.
It was a touching sight, no doubt about it: but the audience, seeing that the play was going no further, grew impatient and began to shout, “We want the play! We want the play!”

All wasted breath, because instead of going on with the performance, the puppets made twice as much noise, and lifting Pinocchio onto their shoulders, carried him in triumph to the lights at the front of the stage.

Then out came the puppet master, a huge man so ugly that the sight of him alone was frightening. He had a great beard as black as an ink scribble, and so long that it reached from his chin to the ground: it is enough to say that when he walked, he stepped on it. His mouth was as wide as an oven, his eyes looked like two red glass lanterns lit from behind; and in his hands he cracked a thick whip made of snakes and fox tails twisted together.
At the puppet master’s unexpected appearance, everyone fell silent: no one made another sound. You could have heard a fly pass. Those poor puppets, male and female, trembled like leaves.
“Why have you come to turn my theatre upside down?” the puppet master asked Pinocchio in the booming voice of an ogre with a terrible head cold.
“Please believe me, most honoured sir, it wasn’t my fault!…”
“That’s enough! Tonight we’ll settle our accounts.”

Sure enough, when the play was over, the puppet master went into the kitchen, where he had prepared a fine sheep for his supper, turning slowly on a roasting spit. And because he had run out of wood to finish cooking and browning it, he called Harlequin and Punchinello and said:
“Bring me that puppet you’ll find hanging on the nail. He looks like a puppet made of very dry wood, and I’m sure that if I throw him on the fire, he’ll give me a splendid blaze for the roast.”

At first Harlequin and Punchinello hesitated; but frightened by a fierce look from their master, they obeyed: and then they returned to the kitchen carrying poor Pinocchio in their arms, while he wriggled like an eel out of water and screamed desperately, “Dad, save me! I don’t want to die, no, I don’t want to die!…”
